title: Four marks
hookLine: the church is one, holy, catholic and apostolic, each tradition explaining how

lines: A WISH, A BOAST, OR A PROMISE?
cards: This Sunday, in a Catholic parish, an Orthodox cathedral and an Anglican chapel, people will stand and say the same old sentence from the Nicene Creed.

It describes the church in four words: one, holy, catholic, apostolic. Then they'll go home to churches that are plainly not one, sometimes not holy, very local, and arguing about what the apostles meant.
So what are they saying? A wish? A boast?
A promise? These four words are the marks of the church: the signs you're meant to recognize it by. Day three hundred six met the small-c catholic.

teach.h: ONE BODY, ONE LORD, ONE BAPTISM.
teach.b: One at a time. One. Paul writes to the Ephesians: "There is one body, and one Spirit, even as ye are called in one hope of your calling; One Lord, one faith, one baptism."
And in John's Gospel Jesus prays "That they all may be one."
Holy. Not because its members are spotless, but because it belongs to God, set apart.
Catholic, small c: universal, for the whole, every place, every people, the whole faith. Apostolic.
Paul says the household of God is "built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone." Now the explanations, side by side.

The Catholic Church teaches that the one church of Christ subsists in the Catholic Church, apostolic through bishops in succession from the apostles, in communion with the pope, while recognizing real elements of the church beyond its walls.

The Orthodox Church holds that it is the one church, kept apostolic by bishops who guard the faith handed down. Anglicans also keep bishops in succession and see themselves within the one catholic church.
Protestant confessions like Augsburg find the church wherever the gospel is rightly preached and the sacraments rightly given; apostolic, for them, means teaching what the apostles taught.
So the same words can describe a visible body with a shape and a history, or a fellowship of believers spread through many churches.
One thing these explanations can share: the marks are said as faith, not as a report card. Christians say them on days when their own church looks nothing like them.

how: Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican, Lutheran and other churches confess the church as one, holy, catholic and apostolic in the Nicene Creed, often aloud together at the Eucharist; each tradition explains the marks in its own way.

o: the four Gospels read at every service
four grades a bishop gives each parish
the creed's four signs that mark out the church

games.q: each mark and its meaning — tap the pairs.
p: one body, one Lord, one baptism
built upon the foundation of the apostles

s: "catholic" in the creed means only the Roman Catholic Church
with a small c it means universal, for the whole. churches across traditions say it.
"holy" means the church's members are spotless
the church is holy because it belongs to God, set apart, not because its members never fail.
Protestant confessions like Augsburg tie the church to the preached gospel and the sacraments
they find the church wherever the gospel is rightly preached and the sacraments rightly given.

games.q: you say "one, holy, catholic, apostolic" on Sunday, but your church is split and struggling. what are you doing?
o: lying, so better to stop saying it.
confessing faith in what the church is in God's eyes and is called to be.
games.why: the marks are said as faith, not a report card. traditions explain them differently, but none says them only on good days.

practice: If you belong to a church, bring it to mind, the building, the faces, the arguments, and run the four words past it: one, holy, catholic, apostolic, noticing which feels thinnest right now.
If you pray, ask for that mark for your church by name. If you don't belong to a church, try the same with any community you're part of: a family, a team, a neighborhood.

wordCard.voice: Four marks. One, holy, catholic and apostolic: the signs of the church in the Nicene Creed, said together, explained differently.

orig.note: Greek: universal, for the whole — the word behind "catholic" in the creed.

carryVoice: Your line: one, holy, catholic, apostolic. Four old words, said together across churches. That's today, done.
